c.v: A roof inspection in Newark, NJ

runs.v: is a systematic evaluation of a roof’s covering, flashing, drainage, ventilation, sealants, deck, and other key components across common Newark roof types, including asphalt shingles, cedar shake, and slate roofs, that rates each area by condition and documents damage, wear, and active-leak indications before water reaches the interior. For homeowners, landlords, property managers, and commercial building owners in Newark and Essex County, these inspections help catch minor issues early before they become expensive repairs, extend roof life, support insurance claims, and protect the property as an investment during maintenance planning or a sale. This page explains the main types of roof inspections, what inspectors check, signs your roof should be inspected, what inspections typically cost, how residential and commercial inspections differ, and why Newark Quality Roofing is chosen for thorough local roof inspection and roof repair services in Newark.

sections.heading: Free Roof Inspection We Provide in Newark, NJ

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing inspects 8 roof components across Essex County: roof-covering materials, including common residential systems such as asphalt shingles, cedar shake, and slate roofs, flashing, penetrations, gutters and drainage, ventilation, sealants, the roof deck, and the attic underside — for residential and commercial properties.

A Newark Quality Roofing inspection starts at the flashing details, because the roofing industry estimates that roughly 90–95% of roof leaks originate at flashing and only 5–10% at the open shingle field, an industry estimate attributed to the NRCA. The NRCA recommends a roof inspection at least twice per year, spring and fall, plus an additional inspection after any major weather event, so a documented inspection history tracks roof condition across the freeze-thaw and storm seasons. Newark roofs must withstand rain, wind, and temperature swings across the year.

and seasonal extremes that stress roofing materials.

— Storm-damage roof inspection documents hail and hidden damage from high winds for an insurance claim, because wind and hail rank as the largest homeowners-insurance claim type at 2.8% of insured homes per year, 1 in 36, per the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I, 2019–2023).

— Real-estate roof inspection assesses roof-covering condition and remaining service life before a home purchase or sale, reporting active-leak indications and component condition per the InterNACHI roof inspection standard of practice.

— Pre-leak moisture inspection uses moisture meters on the deck and attic framing to find trapped moisture before a ceiling stain appears, because sealing the roof deck cuts water intrusion by up to 95%, per the IBHS.

— Commercial low-slope roof inspection checks membrane seams and drainage, because ponding water remaining more than 48 hours counts as a defect and a flat roof needs at least ¼ inch per foot of slope to drain, per the NRCA and ARMA.

— Drone and infrared roof inspection surveys steep and large roofs and locates trapped moisture invisible to the eye, with the infrared cost range named in the cost section, per HomeAdvisor inspection-cost data.

sections.heading: How Our Roofing Contractors Perform Roof Inspection

runs.v: Four-Stage Component Inspection

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing inspectors assess the roof in 4 stages — exterior ground survey, on-roof component inspection, attic-underside inspection, and a written condition report — rating each component and documenting active-leak indications while checking core components such as shingles, flashing, and gutters.

runs.v: A Newark Quality Roofing inspection starts at the flashing because flashing failures are a leading cause of roof leaks in homes, so inspectors look for rust, gaps, or damaged sealant at flashing details, including around chimneys. They also note structural concerns that can affect structural integrity before they turn into larger repair issues. The InterNACHI roof inspection standard of practice directs an inspector to report observed indications of active roof leaks and to describe the roof-covering type, the baseline a Newark Quality Roofing report records.
Moisture Detection and Condition Reporting

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing inspectors measure deck and framing moisture with moisture meters and locate trapped moisture with infrared imaging, finding wet sheathing before a ceiling stain appears.

runs.v: Sealing the roof deck cuts water intrusion by up to 95%, per the IBHS, so a pre-leak inspection identifies a failing detail while a repair stays minor. A Newark Quality Roofing inspector checks attic ventilation against the NRCA and ARMA standard of 1 square foot of net-free vent area per 150 square feet of attic floor, balanced about 50% intake and 50% exhaust, because balanced ventilation extends roof service life by up to 25%, per the NRCA, and proper ventilation also helps prevent ice dams during winter.

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing inspects residential roofs across Essex County, documenting roof-covering condition, flashing, ventilation, and the deck on detached one- and two-family homes with a written report for maintenance, insurance, or a real-estate transaction.

runs.v: Annual inspections are recommended once residential roofs on newark homes are over 15 years old. A detached one- and two-family re-roof or repair of the roof covering counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and requires no construction permit, so a Newark Quality Roofing inspection report documents condition rather than triggering a permit. The report also identifies the roof-covering type, such as asphalt shingles, cedar shake, or slate.

A Newark Quality Roofing storm inspection documents wind and hail damage with timestamped photographs and a component-condition report for an insurance adjuster, because wind and hail rank as the largest homeowners-insurance claim type at 2.8% of insured homes per year, 1 in 36, per the Insurance Information Institute. A roof inspection at the NRCA twice-per-year cadence, spring and fall, helps catch minor leaks early before they turn into costly damage. Annual residential inspections can help newark homeowners avoid costly repairs and save thousands in larger repair bills, and moisture detection can show where a failing detail should be addressed with roof repair while the issue is still minor.

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing inspects commercial low-slope roofs across Essex County, checking EPDM rubber, TPO, and modified-bitumen membrane seams, drainage, and flashing against manufacturer and code condition standards.

runs.v: EPDM lasts 15–25 years, TPO 7–20 years, and modified bitumen 20 years, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart, and EPDM fails most often at the seams while TPO fails at the welded seams.

A Newark Quality Roofing commercial inspection flags ponding water remaining more than 48 hours as a defect, because a flat roof needs at least ¼ inch per foot of slope to drain, per the NRCA and ARMA. On a commercial building, repairing more than 25% of the total roof area in a 12-month period requires a permit under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, so a Newark Quality Roofing inspection report sizes the affected area before a repair scope sets the permit path.

sections.heading: Our Roof Inspection Process, Step by Step

runs.v: Exterior Ground Survey

A Newark Quality Roofing inspector surveys the roof from the ground and the eaves first, identifying obvious flashing, gutter, and roof-covering concerns and planning safe roof access, per the InterNACHI roof inspection standard of practice. Most inspections take 1–2 hours depending on roof size and access. 2. 2
On-Roof Component Inspection

A Newark Quality Roofing inspector examines the roof-covering materials, flashing at every penetration and transition, drainage, and sealants, starting at the flashing details that the roofing industry estimates account for 90–95% of leaks, an industry estimate attributed to the NRCA. 3. 3
Attic and Moisture Inspection

A Newark Quality Roofing inspector checks the deck underside for moisture staining and ventilation, measuring deck and framing moisture with moisture meters, because sealing the roof deck cuts water intrusion by up to 95%, per the IBHS. 4. 4
Documentation and Photography

A Newark Quality Roofing inspector photographs each finding, keys it to a roof diagram, and rates it by urgency, recording roof-covering type and active-leak indications per the InterNACHI roof inspection standard of practice. 5. 5
Written Condition Report

A Newark Quality Roofing inspector delivers a detailed written report with prioritized findings; written report provided includes condition ratings and repair recommendations, along with the documentation an insurance carrier or manufacturer-warranty program accepts, per the Insurance Information Institute.

$75–$600 for most inspections

items.v: A visual roof inspection costs $75–$200, with a national average roof inspection at $248 and a typical range of $125–$377, per HomeAdvisor inspection-cost data.
Pre-purchase inspections cost between $150 and $350.
Formal written inspections typically cost around $350 for homes up to 3,000 sq ft when documentation is needed to support the next roof repair decision.
A drone roof inspection costs $150–$400 for a steep or large roof surveyed from the air, per HomeAdvisor inspection-cost data.
An infrared roof inspection costs $400–$600, the highest-cost method, because infrared imaging locates trapped moisture invisible to the eye, per HomeAdvisor inspection-cost data.
Storm-damage inspections are often free when tied to an insurance claim, including when documenting issues caused by high winds.
Roof inspections in Newark are often free with repairs, and same-week appointments may be available for urgent requests.
Roof size, slope, and accessibility set the inspection cost, because the inspection method is the largest cost factor, per HomeAdvisor.
A documented inspection at the NRCA twice-per-year cadence supports the roughly 25–30% service-life extension that proper maintenance produces, per ARMA.

faqs.q: How often should you inspect a roof in Newark or Essex County?

runs.v: For most properties, we recommend Newark roof inspections twice a year, especially after major storms. An annual inspection is the minimum priority for older systems, and many asphalt shingle roofs in New Jersey have an estimated remaining lifespan of about 15 to 25 years depending on age, installation, and exposure.

faqs.q: How much does a roof inspection cost in Essex County, NJ?

runs.v: Pricing for roof inspection services depends on the type of inspection you need and whether you want a formal written report, a pre-purchase inspection, or a claim-related visit. Contact Newark Quality Roofing for a quote based on the property, roof access, and the purpose of the inspection.

faqs.q: Can a roof inspection find a leak before it appears inside?

runs.v: Yes. Expert roof inspection services can identify damaged areas, flashing problems, drainage issues, and signs of moisture intrusion before water shows up indoors. A pre-purchase inspection can also reveal the true roof condition before buying, which helps you avoid hidden problems and unexpected costs.

faqs.q: Do you need a roof inspection to file a storm-damage insurance claim?

runs.v: In many cases, yes. An inspection documents visible damage and can uncover storm-related issues that are not obvious from the ground, which is important when supporting a claim or planning a repair or replacement project.

faqs.q: What does a roof inspection report cover?

runs.v: A report typically includes findings on shingles, flashing, gutters, visible problem areas, and recommendations for next steps. For hard-to-reach sections or roofs that are unsafe to walk on, we may use drone inspections to document conditions clearly.

faqs.q: Should you repair or replace a roof after an inspection?

runs.v: That depends on the roof’s condition, age, and whether the issues are isolated or widespread. The findings help determine if a targeted repair makes sense, if a full replacement is the better long-term option, or if the roof should move into a replacement project based on wear, structural concerns, and overall remaining life.
